noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know and be able to interpret evidence for the existence of ions, limited to physical properties of ionic compounds, electron density maps and the migration of ions

primer.text: Charged particles announce themselves in three ways: high melting points from a lattice of gripping ions, conductivity that switches on the moment the ions can move, and electrolysis that steers coloured ions toward opposite electrodes. This note walks the giant ionic lattice, its property fingerprint, dissolving in polar water, and the copper chromate demonstration that proves ions exist.

lessons.title: Inside the giant ionic lattice
lessons.opening: An ionic bond is the electrostatic grip between a positive metal cation and a negative non-metal anion, and it pulls in every direction at once. That non-directional attraction packs oppositely charged ions into a giant alternating lattice, whose exact geometry depends on the two ion sizes - sodium chloride and magnesium oxide both settle into cubes.
keyPoints: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion.
The metal atom transfers electrons to the non-metal, charging both particles.
Attraction acts in all directions, which makes ionic bonding non-directional.
Ions stack in a giant alternating lattice; the pattern chosen depends on the two ion sizes.
NaCl and MgO both adopt cubic lattices, and electron-density maps show zero density between the ions.

low.restatement: A metal hands its spare electrons to a non-metal; the two charged particles then tug on each other from every side and settle into a huge alternating stack.
low.analogy: Magnets on a fridge door attract from any angle you approach - ionic attraction likewise ignores direction, so ions pack on all sides.
low.examPointer: Say 'electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions' in full; shortened versions omit the force and lose the mark.

medium.restatement: Electron transfer leaves a cation and an anion whose Coulomb attraction is isotropic, so the lattice grows by alternating charges in three dimensions rather than bonding to one partner.
medium.analogy: Covalent bonding is a handshake with one chosen partner; ionic bonding is a dance hall where everyone attracts everyone of the opposite kind, so a crowd pattern forms.
medium.examPointer: Electron-density maps between Na+ and Cl- fall to zero between the ions - quote this as the evidence that electrons are transferred, not shared.

check.stem: What holds the ions of sodium chloride together in its solid?

options.text: Electrostatic attraction between Na+ cations and Cl- anions
options.explanation: Opposite charges attract in all directions, binding the lattice.

options.text: A shared pair of electrons between each ion pair
options.explanation: Shared pairs describe covalent bonding, not ionic.

options.text: Attraction between ions and free electrons
options.explanation: Delocalised electrons belong to metallic lattices.

options.text: Gravity between the heavy chloride ions
options.explanation: Gravity is negligible beside electrostatic forces here.

check.stem: Why is ionic bonding described as non-directional?

options.text: Each ion attracts every neighbouring oppositely charged ion around it
options.explanation: The Coulomb force has no preferred heading, so bonding spreads in all directions.

options.text: The bond points only along one fixed axis
options.explanation: That would describe a directional covalent bond.

options.text: Ions can only bond to two neighbours
options.explanation: Lattice ions sit surrounded by several oppositely charged neighbours.

options.text: The bond rotates freely at high temperature
options.explanation: Directionality is a geometry statement, not a rotation claim.

check.stem: What does an electron-density map of NaCl show between the two ions?

options.text: Density falls to zero between the ions
options.explanation: No electron population sits midway, the signature of transfer rather than sharing.

options.text: Density peaks midway, marking a shared pair
options.explanation: A midway peak is the covalent signature; NaCl shows the opposite.

options.text: Density is uniform across the whole map
options.explanation: The contours vary, concentrating around each ion.

options.text: Density is only measurable at the nucleus
options.explanation: Contours run over the whole region, not just nuclei.

check.stem: Which factor decides the particular lattice geometry an ionic compound adopts?

options.text: The relative sizes of the positive and negative ions
options.explanation: Ion radii dictate how the alternating spheres can pack.

options.text: The colour of the compound
options.explanation: Colour follows electronic structure, not packing geometry.

options.text: The temperature at which the compound crystallised
options.explanation: Crystal chemistry here is set by ion sizes, not cooling history.

options.text: The number of electrons in the non-metal nucleus
options.explanation: Nuclear electrons do not exist; packing follows ionic radii.

check.stem: MgO and NaCl share which lattice feature?

options.text: Both pack their ions into cubic lattices
options.explanation: The alternating arrangement of similarly sized ion pairs gives cubes in each salt.

options.text: Both contain molecular units of two atoms
options.explanation: Lattice salts are giant structures without discrete molecules.

options.text: Both conduct in the solid state
options.explanation: Fixed ions cannot carry current until melted or dissolved.

options.text: Both need only weak forces to melt
options.explanation: Giant ionic lattices demand high temperatures.

check.stem: Define the ionic bond in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic pull that binds a positively charged metal cation to a negatively charged non-metal anion.

check.stem: Describe the arrangement of ions inside a giant ionic lattice.
check.modelAnswer: Positive and negative ions sit in a regular, repeating, alternating pattern that fills the crystal and leaves it overall electrically neutral.

check.stem: Explain why the electron-density map counts as evidence that NaCl is ionic rather than covalent.
check.modelAnswer: If electrons were shared, density would bridge the two nuclei; instead the map shows each ion holding its own electron population with density dropping to zero in between, which is exactly what complete transfer predicts.

check.stem: A sodium ion has charge +1 and a chloride ion -1. State the overall charge of any sized NaCl crystal fragment and justify with the alternating-packing rule.
check.modelAnswer: Every Na+ is paired against neighbouring Cl- ions in the alternating stack, so positive and negative charges cancel exactly and any crystal fragment carries zero net charge.

lessons.title: Melting, boiling and conducting
lessons.opening: Two everyday behaviours expose the ionic lattice. Oppositely charged ions grip each other so hard that most ionic compounds stay solid until high temperatures, and the bigger the ionic charges the higher those temperatures climb. Yet none of that grip freezes charge movement forever: melt the lattice or dissolve it and the freed ions carry a current.
keyPoints: At room temperature most ionic compounds sit as solids: lattice attractions outmuscle the available thermal energy.
Melting and boiling demand the energy to overcome electrostatic attraction throughout the lattice.
Lattices of more highly charged ions melt at higher temperatures.
Na2O melts at 1405 K while CaO melts at 2845 K thanks to the 2+ versus 1+ cation charge.
Ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved; fixed solid ions cannot move charge.

low.restatement: Salt solids cling together until strong heat, because every ion grips several neighbours; but warm them until molten or pop them into water and the mobile ions instantly conduct.
low.analogy: A velcro wall of alternating hooks: tearing the whole sheet down takes real effort, but once the pieces are loose each one carries a charge flag around the room.
low.examPointer: Conductivity answers need the mobility condition stated - 'molten or in solution' - omitting it loses the mark even if the ions are named.

medium.restatement: Melting an ionic solid means dismantling an extended electrostatic network, and Coulomb's law scales with charge, so CaO with 2+/2- pairs withstands roughly twice the temperature of Na2O's 1+/2- lattice; conductivity then requires ions free to migrate.
medium.analogy: Doubling the magnet strength on every fridge door does not just make one joint harder to break - it hardens every joint across the whole door at once.
medium.examPointer: When comparing Na2O with CaO, quote the charge argument and dismiss size: the two cations are of similar radius, so charge is the deciding factor.

check.stem: Why are most ionic compounds solid at room temperature?

options.text: Electrostatic attractions throughout the lattice exceed the available thermal energy
options.explanation: Room-temperature energy cannot tear the giant lattice apart.

options.text: Covalent bonds inside molecules are unbreakable
options.explanation: Ionic compounds are not molecular; lattice attraction is the relevant force.

options.text: The ions are locked by metallic bonding
options.explanation: Metallic bonding describes metals, not salts.

options.text: Their electrons cannot absorb heat
options.explanation: Heating is absorbed fine; melting is what resists.

check.stem: Melting points of ionic lattices rise when

options.text: the ions carry greater charge, strengthening the lattice-wide attraction
options.explanation: Higher charges pull harder in every direction across the crystal.

options.text: the ions carry smaller charges, easing packing
options.explanation: Smaller charge weakens attraction and lowers melting temperature.

options.text: the compound turns coloured
options.explanation: Colour has no bearing on lattice strength.

options.text: the crystal grows larger
options.explanation: Melting is a per-attraction property, independent of crystal size.

check.stem: Na2O melts at 1405 K and CaO at 2845 K. What dominates this difference?

options.text: The 2+ calcium cation attracts oxide ions harder than the 1+ sodium cation
options.explanation: Charge on the cation doubles the lattice-wide electrostatic grip.

options.text: Calcium ions are far smaller than sodium ions
options.explanation: The two cations are of similar size, so size is explicitly not the factor.

options.text: Oxygen changes oxidation state between the salts
options.explanation: Oxide is O2- in both compounds.

options.text: CaO has weaker attractions but packs tighter
options.explanation: Weaker attraction cannot give the higher melting temperature.

check.stem: Solid potassium bromide will not conduct because

options.text: its ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move to carry charge
options.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles; solid ions vibrate in place.

options.text: its ions carry no charge at all
options.explanation: The ions are charged; they simply cannot migrate.

options.text: electrons in the lattice are bound into pairs
options.explanation: It is the ions, not electron pairs, that would carry current here.

options.text: the crystal reflects charge away from electrodes
options.explanation: No such reflection mechanism exists.

check.stem: Which two states of an ionic compound both conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten and dissolved in solution
options.explanation: Both free the ions to migrate toward the electrodes.

options.text: Solid and molten
options.explanation: Solid ions stay fixed, so the solid fails to conduct.

options.text: Solid and dissolved
options.explanation: Again the solid fails; only solution conducts of the two.

options.text: Gaseous and solid
options.explanation: Neither state provides mobile ions for conduction.

check.stem: State the two states in which an ionic compound conducts electricity.
check.modelAnswer: An ionic compound conducts when molten and when dissolved in solution, because its ions are then free to move and carry charge.

check.stem: State the melting temperatures of sodium oxide and calcium oxide in kelvin.
check.modelAnswer: Na2O melts at 1405 K and CaO melts at 2845 K.

check.stem: Explain why higher ionic charges raise the temperature needed to melt the lattice.
check.modelAnswer: Every ion in a giant lattice pulls on several oppositely charged neighbours, so a larger charge multiplies the strength of all those attractions at once, and much more thermal energy is needed before the whole network can flow.

check.stem: A student tests solid lithium fluoride, molten lithium fluoride and lithium fluoride solution with a lamp circuit. Predict the two setups that light the lamp and give the reason in each case.
check.modelAnswer: The molten sample and the solution light the lamp: melting and dissolving both release Li+ and F- ions from their fixed lattice sites, and only mobile charged particles can carry current.

lessons.title: Dissolving the lattice
lessons.opening: Water dissolves many ionic compounds because its polar molecules do two jobs at once: they prize the lattice apart and then surround each freed ion, positive ends hugging anions and negative ends hugging cations. Whether dissolving succeeds is a tug-of-war between lattice attraction and ion-water attraction - which is why bigger charges usually mean lower solubility.
keyPoints: Many ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents such as water.
Dissolving needs the lattice broken and each ion surrounded by polar molecules.
The delta-positive end of water surrounds anions; the delta-negative end surrounds cations.
Solubility depends on the balance between lattice attraction and ion-water attraction.
Greater ionic charge generally lowers solubility: NaCl 356.9 g per dm3 versus CaCl2 74.4 g per dm3.

low.restatement: Water molecules are tiny dipoles: they yank ions out of the crystal and then crowd around each one, holding it in solution.
low.analogy: A crowd of tiny magnets peeling sticky notes off a board one by one, then each note carried away covered in hands.
low.examPointer: Quote both solubility jobs - breaking the lattice and surrounding the ions - a single-job answer scores half.

medium.restatement: Dissolution is an energy and geometry contest: the Coulomb lattice must be pried open, and hydration shells must form via ion-dipole attraction; heavier charges raise the first cost faster than the second, depressing solubility.
medium.analogy: Bank robbery versus getaway: a bigger vault (higher charge) is harder to crack, and no amount of getaway cars (water molecules) fully compensates.
medium.examPointer: Remember the rule is 'in general' - 356.9 against 74.4 g per dm3 shows the trend, and exceptions exist.

check.stem: Why does water dissolve so many ionic compounds?

options.text: Its polar molecules disrupt the lattice and then surround each ion
options.explanation: Dipole ends attract the ions, prising them loose and keeping them in solution.

options.text: Its molecules share electrons with the ions
options.explanation: No covalent sharing occurs between water and the dissolved ions.

options.text: It reacts chemically with every salt
options.explanation: Dissolving is physical disruption, not reaction with every compound.

options.text: Its neutral molecules slide between ions unnoticed
options.explanation: The dipole attraction is precisely what matters.

check.stem: Which end of a water molecule surrounds a positive cation in solution?

options.text: The delta-negative oxygen end
options.explanation: The partially negative pole is drawn to the positive ion.

options.text: The delta-positive hydrogen end
options.explanation: Like charges repel; the positive pole faces anions instead.

options.text: Either end equally
options.explanation: Orientation is specific: each pole targets its opposite charge.

options.text: No end approaches the cation
options.explanation: Hydration shells form around both ion signs.

check.stem: 356.9 g of NaCl dissolve in one dm3 of water but only 74.4 g of CaCl2. Which rule does this illustrate?

options.text: Greater ionic charge generally lowers an ionic compound's solubility
options.explanation: The 2+ calcium salt laces far less per litre than the 1+ sodium salt.

options.text: Chlorides never dissolve in water
options.explanation: Both salts dissolve; they differ in amount.

options.text: Solubility rises with cation charge
options.explanation: The data shows the opposite direction.

options.text: The two salts have equal solubility
options.explanation: 356.9 and 74.4 differ by nearly five times.

check.stem: Dissolving an ionic crystal requires which two steps?

options.text: Breaking the ionic lattice, then surrounding each ion with polar molecules
options.explanation: Both jobs are done by the polar solvent.

options.text: Melting the crystal, then freezing it into solution
options.explanation: No freeze step exists in dissolution.

options.text: Breaking covalent bonds, then evaporating the solvent
options.explanation: Covalent bonds in the ions survive untouched.

options.text: Ionising the water, then neutralising the ions
options.explanation: Water is already polar; no ionisation step is needed.

check.stem: Solubility of an ionic compound is decided by comparing

options.text: lattice attraction strength against ion-to-polar-molecule attraction
options.explanation: Whichever wins decides whether the crystal dissolves.

options.text: melting point against boiling point
options.explanation: Both describe the dry solid, not dissolution.

options.text: anion size against cation colour
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant; size alone is only part of the lattice side.

options.text: formula mass against crystal mass
options.explanation: Masses do not set the thermodynamic balance.

check.stem: State the two factors on which the solubility of an ionic compound depends.
check.modelAnswer: Breaking down the ionic lattice, and the attraction of polar solvent molecules for the freed ions.

check.stem: Quote the solubilities of NaCl and CaCl2 in grams per dm3 of water.
check.modelAnswer: 356.9 g of NaCl and 74.4 g of CaCl2 each dissolve in one dm3 of water.

check.stem: Explain why a doubly charged cation generally leaves a salt less soluble than a singly charged one.
check.modelAnswer: A 2+ ion binds its neighbours in the lattice with roughly double the electrostatic force, so the lattice is costlier to dismantle, and the ion-dipole attractions of water often cannot make up the difference.

check.stem: Order NaCl, CaCl2, KCl and K2O from most to least soluble using the charge rule and the quoted data, stating the rule at the decision point.
check.modelAnswer: NaCl and KCl (all 1+ cations) sit most soluble, with NaCl at 356.9 g per dm3 quoted; CaCl2 at 74.4 g per dm3 follows as its 2+ cation raises lattice cost; K2O with a 2- oxide paired to two 1+ cations fits the higher-charge, lower-solubility end of the general rule.

lessons.title: Electrolysis as proof
lessons.opening: Electrolysis is the courtroom demonstration that ions exist. Dissolved ions migrate: positive species head for the negative electrode and negative species for the positive one. Copper(II) chromate(VI) makes the migration visible, because its blue Cu2+ and yellow CrO4(2-) ions separate into coloured halos around the two electrodes.
keyPoints: Electrolysis behaviour of ionic substances is clear evidence that ions exist.
In solution, cations swim toward the negative electrode.
In solution, anions swim toward the positive electrode.
Copper(II) chromate(VI) solution holds blue Cu2+ ions and yellow CrO4(2-) ions and looks olive green overall.
On electrolysis, blue appears at the negative electrode and yellow at the positive electrode.

low.restatement: Charged particles in a solution swim toward the electrode of the opposite sign - watching coloured ions split up proves they were charged all along.
low.analogy: Red and blue dancers drift to opposite ends of the hall when music calls two different names; the colour split shows the pair were distinct and charged.
low.examPointer: Map each colour to its electrode explicitly: blue Cu2+ at the negative, yellow chromate at the positive.

medium.restatement: Migration under an electric field is the operational test of charge sign: Cu2+ cations walk to the cathode and colour it blue, while CrO4(2-) anions walk to the anode and colour it yellow, demonstrating both the existence and the sign of the ions.
medium.analogy: A customs queue splits passport-holders by visa type: the field is the queue, and each coloured group reveals which document - which charge - it carries.
medium.examPointer: The olive-green starting colour is the mixture; the split into blue and yellow halos is the observation to quote in answers.

check.stem: Where do positive ions migrate during electrolysis of a solution?

options.text: Toward the negative electrode
options.explanation: Opposite charges attract, so cations travel to the negative pole.

options.text: Toward the positive electrode
options.explanation: That route belongs to the negative ions.

options.text: They stay evenly distributed
options.explanation: The field drives a real separation.

options.text: They collect at both electrodes equally
options.explanation: Each sign has exactly one destination.

check.stem: In the copper(II) chromate(VI) demonstration, which colour marks the positive electrode?

options.text: Yellow, from the chromate anions
options.explanation: CrO4(2-) ions are negative, so they gather at the positive electrode.

options.text: Blue, from copper ions
options.explanation: Cu2+ is positive and heads to the negative electrode.

options.text: Olive green, as at the start
options.explanation: The olive green vanishes as the ions separate.

options.text: No colour appears
options.explanation: The demonstration exists precisely to produce colour halos.

check.stem: Why does copper(II) chromate(VI) suit the migration demonstration?

options.text: Its two ion types carry distinct colours that map onto distinct electrodes
options.explanation: Blue cations versus yellow anions make the separation directly visible.

options.text: Its ions are uncoloured until electrolysis
options.explanation: The ions are coloured before electrolysis; the split is what changes the picture.

options.text: Its ions refuse to move in solution
options.explanation: Migration is the whole point of the demonstration.

options.text: It conducts without any ions
options.explanation: Conduction here happens precisely because ions move.

check.stem: Before electrolysis, copper(II) chromate(VI) solution looks olive green because

options.text: the blue Cu2+ and yellow CrO4(2-) ions are mixed uniformly throughout
options.explanation: An even blend of the two colours reads as olive green.

options.text: a third green ion is present in solution
options.explanation: Only the two coloured ions exist; green is their blend.

options.text: the solution has already undergone electrolysis
options.explanation: The green is the starting state, not the result.

options.text: the electrodes dye the solution
options.explanation: Colour comes from the ions, not the electrodes.

check.stem: What fundamental claim does successful electrolysis of an ionic solution support?

options.text: That mobile charged particles - ions - exist in the solution
options.explanation: Directional migration of coloured species is only explicable if charged ions move.

options.text: That all particles in solution are neutral
options.explanation: Neutral particles would not migrate to electrodes.

options.text: That electrons carry all the current in solutions
options.explanation: In solution the ions are the charge carriers.

options.text: That covalent molecules split at electrodes
options.explanation: The demonstration evidences ions, not covalent splitting.

check.stem: State the electrode destination of cations and of anions during electrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: Positive ions travel to the negative electrode and negative ions travel to the positive electrode.

check.stem: Name the two ions in copper(II) chromate(VI) solution with their colours.
check.modelAnswer: Cu2+ ions are blue and CrO4(2-) ions are yellow.

check.stem: Explain why the colour split in the copper(II) chromate(VI) experiment counts as evidence for ions rather than neutral particles.
check.modelAnswer: Only charged particles respond to an electric field; neutral species would show no electrode-directed migration. The clean separation of blue and yellow toward opposite electrodes therefore demonstrates mobile, sign-carrying ions.

check.stem: Predict and explain what a purple flame of colour would show if a Cu2+ solution were replaced by a colourless Na+ solution alongside yellow chromate, after electrolysis.
check.modelAnswer: No visible halo forms at the negative electrode because Na+ is colourless, yet the yellow chromate still gathers at the positive electrode - migration happens for all ions, colour merely makes it observable.

glossary.definition: A positively charged ion, formed when a metal atom loses electrons.
A negatively charged ion, formed when a non-metal atom gains electrons.
The passage of current through a solution or melt that drives ions to the electrode of opposite sign.
The pull between a dissolved ion and the charged end of a polar solvent molecule such as water.
